html:
The laminar models reviewed above describe how error signals are computed and routed across populations of neurons organized into layers and thalamocortical loops. But populations are composed of individual neurons, each equipped with thousands to tens of thousands (e.g., ∼\sim5k–30k depending on layer/species) of synapses distributed across a morphologically complex dendritic tree, endowed with compartment-specific nonlinearities, and subject to distinct local plasticity rules at different dendritic locations. Understanding how error signals are computed at the single-neuron level is not merely a matter of finer resolution; it determines what comparison operations must be physically instantiated by dendritic and synaptic biophysics, what signals must be co-localized at each synapse for learning rules to approximate gradient descent on the global objective, and whether the brain requires separate "error neuron" populations or whether error computation can be folded into the dendritic machinery of ordinary pyramidal cells. Below, we examine several complementary proposals for how individual neurons participate in error-signal generation, beginning with the per-unit error computations implied by standard predictive coding, then advancing to multi-compartment dendritic models that exploit the pyramidal neuron’s biophysical architecture, and finally considering self-predictive, constraint-based, metabolic, and homeostatic signals that round out the effective error landscape at each cortical neuron.

In canonical predictive coding, the per-neuron error computation falls directly from the global free-energy decomposition (under Laplace/Gaussian assumptions) described in "Cortical Loss Functions." Each "representation unit" jj at level ll–mapped onto deep-layer (L5/6) pyramidal cells in the Bastos et al. canonical microcircuit 1–updates its activity μj(l)\mu_j^{(l)} by integrating two error-driven signals: A 2026 model compares error-neuron microcircuits with predictive-coding networks (Figure) 33. The model can implement predictive coding (Figure).

μ̇j(l)=−Πj(l)εj(l)+∑k∂gk(l−1)∂μj(l)Πk(l−1)εk(l−1),\begin{equation} \dot{\mu}_j^{(l)} \;=\; -\,\Pi_j^{(l)}\,\varepsilon_j^{(l)} \;+\; \sum_k \frac{\partial g_k^{(l-1)}}{\partial \mu_j^{(l)}}\; \Pi_k^{(l-1)}\,\varepsilon_k^{(l-1)}, \end{equation} where the first term is the precision-weighted prediction error at the neuron’s own level—arising because μj(l)\mu_j^{(l)} deviates from the top-down prediction gj(𝝁(l+1))g_j(\boldsymbol{\mu}^{(l+1)})–and the second is the Jacobian-weighted, precision-scaled prediction error propagated from the level below, capturing the extent to which the bottom-up prediction errors at level l−1l{-}1 are attributable to μj(l)\mu_j^{(l)} through the generative function g(l−1)g^{(l-1)} 2, 3, 4. Importantly, both signals are locally available in principle: the top-down error arrives via feedback connections, while the bottom-up error arrives via feedforward connections–conforming to the laminar routing architecture described above. Each "error unit" at level ll–mapped onto superficial (L2/3) pyramidal cells–computes εj(l)=μj(l)−gj(𝝁(l+1))\varepsilon_j^{(l)} = \mu_j^{(l)} - g_j(\boldsymbol{\mu}^{(l+1)}); its output is the error signal: a well-predicted state drives the error unit toward silence, whereas a poorly predicted state drives vigorous firing that propagates the mismatch upward through the hierarchy. The individual representation neuron therefore operates under dual error-driven pressure: it must simultaneously satisfy the top-down prior (reducing the prediction error imposed on it from above) and account for the evidence from below (reducing the prediction errors it causes at the next level down). This dual pressure–conform to expectations from above while explaining evidence from below–is the single-neuron signature of hierarchical Bayesian error correction.

However, this formulation treats neurons as point units: each is a scalar value with a single input–output function and no internal spatial structure. For a point neuron, the error signals it sends and receives are scalar mismatches, and learning requires only that a Hebbian-like plasticity rule at the synapses implementing glg_l is modulated by presynaptic activity and the postsynaptic error εl\varepsilon_l 4, 5. This is the mathematical ideal. But cortical pyramidal neurons are not points; they are spatially extended, electrically compartmentalized structures with multiple semi-independent integration zones and a rich repertoire of active dendritic conductances (see "The Fundamentals" and 6, 7). The central question for neuronal error computation is therefore whether the multi-compartment architecture of real pyramidal neurons can be exploited to implement richer error-signal generation than point-neuron predictive coding envisions— and, if so, whether these dendritic computations can subsume the role of dedicated error-neuron populations (which are required to compute ε\varepsilon in the 2012 "canonical" account), folding error computation into the internal structure of the very neurons that also carry predictions. A 2026 model tests the effect of spike-timing jitter (Figure) 36. Dendritic plateaus improve robustness in a simulated network (Figure).

A rapidly growing family of models answers this question affirmatively: the functional separation between basal/perisomatic and apical dendritic compartments of pyramidal neurons provides a biophysical substrate for computing per-neuron error signals—and, in several formulations, for approximating the error signals that backpropagation would require, using only locally available information 8, 9, 10, 11. The core idea, common to all such models, is deceptively simple. The basal and perisomatic dendrites, which receive primarily feedforward and local recurrent input, compute a "bottom-up drive"—what the neuron would produce given current input alone. The apical tuft dendrites, which receive primarily top-down feedback and contextual input in layer 1, convey a "teaching" or "target" signal—what the neuron should produce given higher-level context. The mismatch between these two compartmental voltages serves as a per-neuron error signal that can drive synaptic plasticity at feedforward synapses. Different models formalize this intuition with different biophysical and mathematical assumptions and arrive at different plasticity rules, but the underlying architectural motif is shared: the pyramidal neuron is a biological comparator, and the apical–basal voltage difference is the local error signal.

An early and influential formalization of how compartmentalization enables local error computation was provided by Urbanczik and Senn 12. Their model neuron has just two compartments—a dendritic compartment whose potential VwV_w is set by plastic synaptic weights, and a somatic compartment whose potential UU integrates dendritic drive with additional proximal ("nudging") input. The central construct is the dendritic prediction Vw*V^*_w: the somatic potential that would obtain if all proximal input were silenced. They identify the key local error signal as the instantaneous spike-rate prediction error: A review illustrates a dendritic error model (Figure) 34. The same review contrasts dendritic and predictive-coding models (Figure).

S(t)−ϕ(Vw*(t))\begin{equation} S(t) - \phi(V^*_w(t)) \end{equation} where S(t)S(t) is the somatic spike train. This is the key conceptual move: the neuron’s own spikes become the teaching signal, and the dendrite’s predicted firing probability becomes the local “expectation”—so the comparator is intra-neuronal (dendrite ↔\leftrightarrow soma), not a separate error population. This error enters synaptic change through their plasticity induction variable at each dendritic synapse ii: PIi(t)=(S(t)−ϕ(Vw*))h(Vw*(t))∂V𝒘(t)∂wi,\begin{equation} PI_i(t) = \bigl(S(t) - \phi(V^*_w)\bigr)\,h(V^*_w(t))\, \frac{\partial V_{\mathbf{w}}(t)}{\partial w_i}, \end{equation} where h(Vw*(t))=ϕ′(Vw*)ϕ(Vw*)h(V^*_w(t)) = \frac{\phi'(V^*_w)}{\phi(V^*_w)} is a positive gain factor that normalizes plasticity by the current predicted firing rate. Depending on the source of the direct input into the soma, the same dendritic error signal supports different learning regimes. They also make the unification claim explicit: if a reward signal modulates the learning rate, the same mechanism implements reinforcement learning—i.e., one compartmental prediction-error rule spanning supervised, unsupervised, and RL regimes. Urbanczik and Senn demonstrated that this single rule, without modification, could learn a supervised input–output mapping at the single-neuron level, support associative memory formation in a recurrent network (in which nudging patterns are delivered via somatic synapses during learning and subsequently recalled from dendritic input alone), and drive unsupervised self-organization of topographic maps (when the nudging arises from lateral recurrent connectivity within the network itself, so that the network computes its own teaching signal).

Importantly, this model does not invoke the specific apical-basal morphology of pyramidal neurons—the dendritic compartment is generic, and the error signal arises from the separation between any dendritic predictor and the somatic output it attempts to forecast, rather than from a comparison between distinct input streams (e.g., bottom-up vs. top-down) arriving at morphologically segregated dendritic domains. This generality is a strength, not a limitation: by showing that compartmentalization alone—the minimal departure from the point-neuron assumption afforded by splitting a neuron into two electrically coupled but functionally distinguishable compartments—suffices for a biological neuron to compute a local error signal adequate for exact gradient-based credit assignment using only locally available quantities, Urbanczik and Senn established what is arguably the central theoretical result underlying the entire "dendritic error computation" research program. The subsequent models discussed below can be understood as instantiating this core principle—that the mismatch between what a dendritic compartment predicts and what the soma actually does constitutes an error signal sufficient for hierarchical credit assignment—in the specific anatomical configuration of cortical pyramidal cells, mapping feedforward and feedback streams onto the basal and apical dendritic compartments respectively and thereby connecting single-neuron error computation to error routing across cortical areas 9, 10, 11.

Sacramento, Costa, Bengio, and Senn proposed an influential a model in which error signals are encoded directly in the apical dendritic compartments of pyramidal neurons, eliminating the need for a separate population of dedicated error-coding cells and allowing the same neuron to simultaneously propagate activity (at the soma) and represent error (at the apical dendrite) 9. The model builds on the dendritic predictive plasticity framework of Urbanczik and Senn, which derived a local synaptic learning rule from the principle that a dendritic compartment predicts the neuron’s somatic spiking output and updates its synapses to reduce the prediction error between somatic activity and dendritic expectation 12. Sacramento et al. extend this single-neuron principle to a multilayer network by exploiting the three-compartment organization of neocortical pyramidal cells–basal dendrites, soma, and apical dendrites–as three functionally distinct integration zones that together implement a local error-computation circuit within each neuron. A related preprint tests top-down signaling across layers (Figure). The preprint investigates independent feedforward and feedback learning (Figure). The preprint evaluates dendritic target propagation (Figure).

Each hidden-layer pyramidal neuron is modeled as a three-compartment unit. The basal compartment vB,kPv_{B,k}^P (P=pyramidal, B=basal, k=layer index) receives bottom-up (feedforward) input from pyramidal cells in the layer below via weights Wk,k−1PW_{k,k-1}^P, encoding the neuron’s current prediction of its own activity based on ascending drive. The apical compartment vA,kPv_{A,k}^P integrates two opposing signals: (i) top-down feedback from pyramidal cells in the layer above via weights Wk,k+1PPW_{k,k+1}^PP, and (ii) lateral inhibitory input from local SST-like interneurons via weights Wk,kPIW_{k,k}PI. The soma ukPu_k^P integrates basal and apical contributions through conductance-based dynamics: A related preprint models cellular and dendritic specialization (Figure) 35.

ddtukP=−glkukP+gB(vB,kP−ukP)+gA(vA,kP−ukP),\begin{equation} \frac{d}{dt}u_k^P \;=\; -g_{lk}\,u_k^P \;+\; g_B\,(v_{B,k}^P - u_k^P)\;+\; g_A\,(v_{A,k}^P - u_k^P), \end{equation} where gBg_B and gAg_A are the effective transfer conductances coupling basal and apical compartments to the soma, respectively. This conductance-based formulation ensures that apical input acts as a modulatory influence on somatic output: when the apical compartment is at rest (vA,k≈0v_{A,k}\approx0), the soma is driven primarily by the basal (feedforward) prediction; when apical voltage deviates from rest, it additively shifts somatic membrane potential, modulating the neuron’s firing rate. The apical compartment voltage is determined by the sum of top-down feedback and lateral inhibition: vA,kP=Wk,k+1PPϕ(uk+1P)+Wk,kPIϕ(ukI)\begin{equation} v_{A,k}^P=W_{k,k+1}^{PP}\phi(u_{k+1}^P)\;+\;W_{k,k}^{PI}\phi(u_k^I) \end{equation} where ϕ\phi is the neuronal transfer function (a nonlinear function) and ukIu_k^I are the somatic potentials of the interneurons at the same layer. The key architectural insight is that this apical voltage will register a non-zero signal–an error–only when the top-down feedback from the layer above is not fully cancelled by the lateral interneurons. This transforms the apical dendrite from a passive recipient of feedback into an active error-encoding compartment.

The lateral interneurons within each hidden layer serve a specific and critical function: they learn to predict–and thereby cancel–the top-down feedback that the network generates internally. Each interneuron is modeled as a two-compartment unit that receives lateral input from same-layer pyramidal cells on its dendrites (via weights Wk,kIPW_{k,k}^{IP}) and a weak "nudging" teaching signal from the corresponding pyramidal neuron in the layer above. Through plasticity at these lateral synapses (driven by the same dendritic prediction-error principle), interneurons learn to reproduce the activity of the upper-layer pyramidal population as a function of the current layer’s pyramidal activity–effectively learning the same input-output mapping as the feedforward pathway one level up. Once this mapping is acquired, the inhibitory projections from interneurons back to the apical dendrites of same-layer pyramidal cells (Wk,kPIW_{k,k}^{PI}) learn to exactly negate the excitatory top-down feedback (Wk,k+1PPW_{k,k+1}^{PP}), driving the apical compartment to its resting potential. Sacramento et al. term the resulting network state self-predicting: in the absence of any external teaching signal at the output layer, the lateral microcircuit fully explains (cancels) all internally generated top-down activity, rendering apical dendrites silent throughout the network. The self-predicting state is the equilibrium from which learning-relevant error signals emerge as deviations, and Sacramento et al. propose that its establishment could occur during a developmental period–consistent with the developmental maturation of excitatory-inhibitory balance observed experimentally 13. The plasticity rule governing interneuron-to-pyramidal synapses Wk,kPIW_{k,k}^{PI} has a particularly intuitive form: it drives the apical compartment voltage toward rest, Δ𝑾k,kPI∝(𝒗rest−𝒗A,kP)(𝒓kI)T\Delta \mathbf{W}_{k,k}^{\mathrm{PI}} \propto (\mathbf{v}_{\mathrm{rest}} - \mathbf{v}_{\mathrm{A},k}^{\mathrm{P}})\,(\mathbf{r}_{k}^{\mathrm{I}})^{T}–a dendritic variant of homeostatic inhibitory plasticity 14 that can be read as: "adjust inhibitory synapses until the apical dendrite is silenced." A preprint tests dendritic target propagation (Figure).

The computational power of the self-predicting state is revealed when a novel teaching signal is presented at the output layer–modeled as a somatic nudging current that pushes output-layer pyramidal neurons toward a desired target uNtrgtu_N^{trgt}. This nudging creates a discrepancy between the output the network would have produced on the basis of its feedforward weights alone and the target, shifting output-layer firing rates. Because the lateral interneurons have learned to predict only the self-generated top-down feedback (i.e., the feedback the network would produce without nudging), the now-altered top-down signal arriving at the apical dendrites of the penultimate hidden layer can no longer be fully cancelled. The residual–the mismatch between the nudged top-down feedback and the interneuron’s cancellation signal–appears as a non-zero apical voltage deflection 𝒗A,kP≠0\mathbf{v}_{\mathrm{A},k}^{\mathrm{P}} \neq 0. This deflection is the error signal. It propagates from the apical compartment down to the soma via the apical coupling conductance gAg_A, where it modulates the neuron’s firing rate and thereby induces plasticity at the basal (feedforward) synapses. Importantly, this error signal is neuron-specific: each pyramidal neuron receives a different top-down signal (weighted by its own column of 𝑾k,k+1PP\mathbf{W}_{k,k+1}^{\mathrm{PP}}) and has a different residual after interneuron cancellation, so the error is spatially resolved across the population–implementing unit-specific credit assignment without requiring a separate error-neuron population.

All plastic synapses in the model obey a common form of dendritic predictive plasticity: ddtw=η(ϕ(u)−ϕ(v))r,\frac{d}{dt}w = \eta\,\bigl(\phi(u) - \phi(v)\bigr)\,r, where uu and vv are somatic and dendritic compartment potentials, respectively, and rr is the presynaptic firing rate. For basal (feedforward) synapses on pyramidal neurons, the learning rule compares somatic firing rate ϕ(𝒖kP)\phi(\mathbf{u}_{k}^{\mathrm{P}}) against the rate predicted by the basal dendritic compartment alone, ϕ(𝒗̂B,kP)\phi(\hat{\mathbf{v}}_{\mathrm{B},k}^{\mathrm{P}}) (where 𝒗̂B,kP\hat{\mathbf{v}}_{\mathrm{B},k}^{\mathrm{P}} is the basal potential attenuated by dendritic conductance ratios). In the self-predicting state without nudging, soma and basal prediction agree (ukP=v̂B,kPu_k^P=\hat{v}_{\mathrm{B},k}^{\mathrm{P}}), yielding zero plasticity induction–the network is at a fixed point. When a teaching signal is present, the apical error perturbs the soma away from the basal prediction, and the resulting discrepancy ϕ(𝒖kP)−ϕ(𝒗̂B,kP)\phi(\mathbf{u}_{k}^{\mathrm{P}}) - \phi(\hat{\mathbf{v}}_{\mathrm{B},k}^{\mathrm{P}})) drives weight updates in a direction that reduces the output-layer mismatch. The key biological virtue of this rule is that it depends only on quantities locally available at the synapse: the postsynaptic somatic firing rate, the local dendritic branch potential, and the presynaptic input–consistent with the phenomenology of voltage-dependent and STDP-like plasticity (covered in the next section "Cortical Plasticity") 15, 16. A related model compares biologically motivated plasticity rules (Figure).

Sacramento et al. prove analytically that, in the weak-feedback limit (λ→0\lambda\rightarrow0, where λ\lambda is a parameter controlling the strength of top-down and teaching inputs relative to bottom-up drive), the synaptic weight updates prescribed by their dendritic plasticity rules converge to the weight changes computed by the backpropagation algorithm. Specifically, the somatic potential of a hidden-layer neuron decomposes into a feedforward term plus a backpropagated error term:

𝒖kP=𝒖k−+λN−k+1𝑾k,k+1PP(∏l=k+1N−1𝑫l−𝑾l,l+1PP)𝑫N−(𝒖Ntrgt−𝒖N−)+𝒪(λN−k+2),\begin{equation} \mathbf{u}_{k}^{\mathrm{P}} = \mathbf{u}_{k}^{-} + \lambda^{N-k+1}\,\mathbf{W}_{k,k+1}^{\mathrm{PP}}\!\left(\prod_{l=k+1}^{N-1}\mathbf{D}_{l}^{-}\,\mathbf{W}_{l,l+1}^{\mathrm{PP}}\right)\mathbf{D}_{N}^{-}\!\left(\mathbf{u}_{N}^{\mathrm{trgt}} - \mathbf{u}_{N}^{-}\right) + \mathcal{O}(\lambda^{N-k+2}), \end{equation} where uk−u_k^- is the activation of the purely feedforward network (obtained by removing all top-down and lateral connections), Dl−D_l^- is a diagonal matrix of transfer-function derivatives evaluated at ul−u_l^-, and the product of 𝑫l−𝑾l,l+1PP\mathbf{D}_{l}^{-}\,\mathbf{W}_{l,l+1}^{\mathrm{PP}} matrices is exactly the chain of Jacobians that backpropagation computes when propagating the output error (uNtrgt−uN−u_N^{trgt}-u_N^-) backward through the network. The resulting weight update for feedforward synapses from layer k−1 to layer k becomes: Δ𝑾k,k−1PP=ηk,k−1λN−k+1(∏l=kN−1𝑫l−𝑾l,l+1PP)𝑫N−(𝒖Ntrgt−𝒖N−)(𝒓k−1−)T+𝒪(λN−k+2),\begin{equation} \Delta\mathbf{W}_{k,k-1}^{\mathrm{PP}} = \eta_{k,k-1}\,\lambda^{N-k+1}\!\left(\prod_{l=k}^{N-1}\mathbf{D}_{l}^{-}\,\mathbf{W}_{l,l+1}^{\mathrm{PP}}\right)\mathbf{D}_{N}^{-}\!\left(\mathbf{u}_{N}^{\mathrm{trgt}} - \mathbf{u}_{N}^{-}\right)\!\left(\mathbf{r}_{k-1}^{-}\right)^{T} + \mathcal{O}(\lambda^{N-k+2}), \end{equation} which, up to the scalar factor λN−k\lambda^{N-k} (absorbable into the learning rate), equals the backpropagation weight change–provided the top-down weights equal the transpose of the corresponding feedforward weights. This weight-symmetry requirement is, of course, the classical weight-transport problem. Sacramento et al. address it in two complementary ways: (i) when top-down weights are set randomly and held fixed, the model implements feedback alignment 17, in which forward weights align over learning to make use of the fixed random feedback; (ii) when top-down weights are made plastic according to a local rule that minimizes an inverse reconstruction loss, the model implements a form of target propagation 18, 19, in which the feedback pathway learns to approximately invert the forward pathway. In either case, exact weight symmetry is not required for successful learning in practice.

A distinctive feature of the Sacramento et al. model relative to prior biologically oriented deep-learning proposals is that it operates continuously in time with all plasticity rules always active–there is no need for alternating between a "free" phase (network running freely) and a "clamped" phase (target imposed), as required by contrastive Hebbian learning 20 and equilibrium propagation 21, or between distinct temporal phases in which apical activity is compared with and without the teaching input 10. Instead, the simultaneous presence of top-down feedback (carrying the teaching-induced perturbation) and lateral inhibition (carrying the self-prediction that should cancel the unperturbed feedback) at the apical dendrite provides a spatial rather than temporal difference: the error is represented as a concurrent voltage deflection in one compartment, not as a subtraction across two time windows. This spatial encoding of error is continuously available to drive plasticity at all feedforward synapses simultaneously, making the model compatible with the brain’s apparent lack of globally synchronized learning phases. In their simulations, Sacramento et al. demonstrate that the model can learn a nonlinear regression task (approximating a random multilayer teacher network) and classify MNIST handwritten digits (achieving 1.96% test error with a 784-500-500-10-neuron network architecture)–performance comparable to feedback alignment and target propagation baselines (~1.6-2.4%) and substantially better than a shallow learner that updates only the output-layer weights (8.4%), confirming that the dendritic error signals propagate useful credit-assignment information to deep hidden layers.

The Sacramento et al. model resonates with several architectural motifs identified in the preceding laminar-error-signal account, while also introducing distinctive commitments. The use of SST-like interneurons targeting apical dendrites to provide a cancellation signal aligns closely with the Bastos et al. canonical microcircuit’s assignment of SST+^+ cells to the inhibitory component of the top-down prediction 1, and with the empirical observation that prediction errors in mouse visual cortex arise from a failure to locally inhibit feedback 22, 23. The model’s three-compartment pyramidal architecture directly exploits the same dendritic compartmentalization–basal for feedforward drive, apical for feedback/contextual input–that undergirds the apical-dendritic precision-gating mechanism detailed above; the apical Ca2+^{2+} electrogenesis reviewed in that context provides a biophysical substrate by which the weak conductance-based apical-to-soma coupling assumed in the model (gAg_A) could be amplified or gated in a state-dependent manner, linking the model’s error propagation to the precision-weighting architecture. There is also a notable alignment with the predictive routing framework 24: in both, "error" is not computed by a dedicated subtractor neuron but emerges from the differential effect of top-down signals on pyramidal activity–in predictive routing via oscillatory-inhibitory preparation of specific feedforward channels, in Sacramento et al. via the homeostatic interneuron cancellation of self-predicted feedback. However, Sacramento et al. depart from canonical predictive coding in an important respect: whereas Bastos et al. assign superficial pyramidal cells (L2/3) the role of error units whose firing rate encodes εl\varepsilon_l, Sacramento et al. encode error in the apical dendritic voltage of pyramidal neurons that also carry the representational signal at their soma. This means the same neuron simultaneously represents the posterior expectation (somatic rate) and the error (apical voltage), collapsing the two-population architecture of canonical predictive coding into a single multi-compartment cell. Whether this dual-use encoding is realized biologically–or whether cortex maintains at least a partial segregation into error-dominant and representation-dominant subpopulations–remains an open empirical question, but the dendritic model demonstrates that such segregation is not computationally necessary for backprop-approximate credit assignment, provided that the neuron’s morphological complexity is taken into account.

The models reviewed above represent the apical error signal as a graded voltage deflection—a continuous, analog mismatch that weakly modulates somatic firing rate through a linear conductance coupling gAg_A. But cortical pyramidal neurons, particularly the thick-tufted L5 cells central to corticothalamic and corticofugal output, possess regenerative dendritic conductances that can transform such graded mismatches into discrete, all-or-none events: dendritic calcium spikes and plateau potentials. These events—and the somatic burst firing they trigger—constitute a qualitatively different error-signaling regime: high-amplitude, temporally extended, and sharply distinguished from background single-spike activity. The biophysical substrate is the BAC (backpropagation-activated calcium) firing mechanism 7: when a backpropagating somatic action potential coincides with sufficient depolarization at the apical calcium spike initiation zone (at the main apical trunk bifurcation), a regenerative calcium spike is triggered that propagates to the soma and elicits a high-frequency burst of action potentials. Importantly, this requires the conjunctive presence of bottom-up drive (sufficient for a somatic spike) and top-down input (sufficient to depolarize the apical tuft)–precisely the conjunction that, in the Sacramento et al. framework, corresponds to a non-zero apical compartment voltage following incomplete interneuron cancellation of feedback.

The burst/singlet distinction maps directly onto the error-signal framework: in the self-predicting state, apical dendrites are near rest and neurons fire isolated spikes driven by feedforward input alone—the "no error" regime. When a teaching signal or prediction violation creates an uncompensated apical depolarization that exceeds the calcium spike threshold, the resulting dendritic spike triggers burst firing—the "error present" regime. This discrete transition offers several advantages over graded voltage encoding as an error signal. First, high signal-to-noise ratio: dendritic calcium spikes produce strong depolarizations and drive somatic bursts with short (<10ms) inter-spike intervals that are readily distinguishable from single spikes by downstream neurons, providing a robust signal that does not require fine rate discrimination. Second, temporal extension: dendritic plateau potentials persist for∼\sim50-200+ms–an order of magnitude longer than axonal spikes–generating sustained, compartment-specific calcium transients that can engage the calcium-dependent enzymatic cascades underlying synaptic modification (detailed in "Cortical Plasticity"). As Burger, Rule, and O’Leary demonstrate, this extended timescale also confers robustness to timing jitter: dendritic plateau potentials enable reliable coincidence detection even when afferent spikes arrive with the millisecond-scale temporal variability characteristic of cortical networks, ensuring that the error signal is not degraded by the asynchrony inherent in biological spike trains 25. Third, nonlinear thresholding: the regenerative nature of the calcium spike imposes a sharp activation threshold, so that weak apical mismatches produce only subthreshold graded modulation while strong mismatches trigger the full burst response–effectively implementing a form of precision-dependent error gating, in which only sufficiently confident error signals elicit the discrete burst event that commands synaptic plasticity. This thresholding has a natural Bayesian interpretation: low-precision (small, uncertain) prediction errors are filtered out at the dendritic level, while high-precision (large, reliable) errors are amplified into unambiguous instructive signals. Leugering, Nieters, and Pipa further show that the interaction of localized plateau potentials across functionally compartmentalized dendritic branches enables neurons to integrate spike sequences across behavioral timescales far exceeding passive membrane time constants, suggesting that dendritic nonlinearities can sustain error representations across the temporal gaps that separate predictions from their sensory confirmation 26.

The relationship between dendritic spike-based error signaling and the graded-voltage models discussed above is one of refinement and amplification, not contradiction. Sacramento et al.’s linear apical-to-soma coupling can be understood as a first-order approximation to a system that, in biological neurons, includes a nonlinear amplification stage: subthreshold apical input produces the weak, continuous rate modulation the model assumes, while suprathreshold input engages regenerative calcium electrogenesis and triggers the discrete burst regime. The apical amplification mechanism and its thalamic/neuromodulatory gating discussed in the laminar-error-signals section ("Apical-dendritic Ca2+^{2+} electrogenesis") provides the biophysical means by which this threshold can be dynamically adjusted—raising it in conditions of high uncertainty (suppressing error propagation when feedback is unreliable) and lowering it during states of high arousal or attention (facilitating error-driven learning when feedback is informative). In this view, the graded and discrete error-signaling modes are not alternatives but two regimes of a single dendritic mechanism, with the calcium spike threshold serving as a controllable gate that determines when an apical mismatch is sufficiently salient to be broadcast as a burst-encoded error signal to downstream plasticity machinery and postsynaptic targets.

The instructive error signals reviewed above–dendritic apical-basal voltage mismatches, burst-encoded calcium-spike errors–convey specific information about how a neuron’s output should change to reduce a global task or inference objective. But cortical neurons are simultaneously subject to intrinsic error signals that arise not from mismatches between neural output and an external reference, but from deviations of the neuron’s own operational state from internally maintained set points. The most extensively characterized is the firing-rate homeostatic error: the discrepancy between a neuron’s time-averaged activity ⟨r⟩τ\langle r \rangle_\tau and a cell-type-specific target rate r*r^*. Intracellular calcium concentration provides the biophysical readout, integrating spike-driven calcium influx over timescales of hours to days; calcium-sensing molecular cascades then transduce the mismatch into bidirectional adjustments of synaptic strength and intrinsic excitability 27, 28. From a loss-function perspective, this machinery performs approximate gradient descent on a homeostatic penalty ℒhomeo∝(⟨r⟩τ−r*)2\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{homeo}} \propto (\langle r \rangle_\tau - r^*)^2. Notably, the same ionic species–calcium–serves as the error currency for both the fast instructive signal (dendritic calcium spikes encoding apical mismatch on sub-second timescales, as reviewed above) and the slow homeostatic signal (time-averaged calcium concentration tracking mean rate over hours), with the two error channels distinguished by timescale and subcellular compartment rather than by molecular identity. The specific mechanisms by which homeostatic error reshapes synapses–synaptic scaling, metaplastic threshold shifts, intrinsic excitability regulation–are deferred to "Cortical Plasticity"; the essential point here is that homeostatic error constitutes an always-on background signal at every cortical neuron, constraining the operating regime within which instructive learning occurs and ensuring that weight modifications driven by task-relevant errors do not push neurons into pathological silence or saturation where gradient information is lost.

A more dynamic generalization of this homeostatic principle is developed by Luczak and colleagues in the "neurons learn by predicting future activity" framework 29. Rather than comparing current activity against a fixed set point, each neuron is posited to predict its own future activity–its firing pattern at the next time step or over a short temporal horizon–on the basis of its current pattern of synaptic inputs. The local error signal then becomes a temporal self-prediction error: the discrepancy between what the neuron predicted it would do and what it actually does. This objective is entirely local (depending only on quantities available at the single neuron) and unsupervised (requiring no external teaching signal or top-down feedback). Luczak et al. demonstrate that this principle, applied uniformly across a network, accounts for a range of empirically observed plasticity phenomena–including stimulus selectivity, temporal sequence learning, and response normalization–and interpret it as a single-neuron temporal instantiation of predictive processing: just as the cortical hierarchy minimizes prediction error across levels, each neuron minimizes the prediction error of its own future state. Classical homeostatic regulation then emerges as a limiting case: when the predicted future activity is time-invariant, the self-predictive error reduces to comparison against a constant target rate. When the prediction is input-dependent and temporally structured, the error signal captures stimulus-specific and sequential regularities beyond mean-rate deviation, blurring the boundary between homeostatic maintenance and representation learning. This self-predictive temporal error coexists with, and complements, the instructive dendritic errors reviewed above: the apical-basal voltage mismatch conveys what higher-level context demands of the neuron (an externally imposed error), while the self-predictive signal reflects the neuron’s own temporal model of its input statistics (an internally generated error). A related "prospective" minimization principle appears in the neuronal least-action framework of Senn et al., where pyramidal neuron voltage dynamics are posited to prospectively minimize the local somato-dendritic mismatch error within each neuron–implementing a form of anticipatory error reduction that bridges instructive and self-predictive objectives 30. Metabolic constraints impose a final class of per-neuron error signal. Cortical computation is energetically costly–action potentials, synaptic vesicle cycling, and ionic-gradient maintenance claim a disproportionate share of the brain’s∼\sim20W power budget 31–and neural codes show pervasive evidence of pressure to minimize metabolic expenditure for a given level of information transmission 32. At the single-neuron level, this pressure is captured by a metabolic penalty ℒmetabolic∝c(ri)\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{metabolic}} \propto c(r_i) that increases with firing rate, favoring sparse, low-rate codes and serving as the biological counterpart of the L1/L2 regularization terms that prevent overfitting in artificial networks. Biophysically, metabolic state is read out through local molecular sensors–ATP/ADP ratio, extracellular adenosine released in proportion to synaptic activity, and astrocyte-neuron lactate shuttle dynamics–that modulate both synaptic efficacy and intrinsic excitability. Together, homeostatic set-point errors, self-predictive temporal errors, and metabolic costs define a background error landscape that each cortical neuron inhabits independently of any task-specific teaching signal. The effective per-neuron loss can therefore be understood as a composite: an instructive component (dendritic mismatch) driving credit assignment across levels, a homeostatic component (rate deviation from set point) preventing destabilization, a self-predictive component (temporal prediction error) promoting efficient encoding of input statistics, and a metabolic component (activity cost) enforcing representational parsimony. The interplay among these error channels–particularly how homeostatic and metabolic state modulate the gain, threshold, and direction of instructive plasticity through metaplastic mechanisms–is taken up in "Cortical Plasticity." The neuron-level proposals reviewed above converge on a central insight: the morphological complexity of cortical pyramidal neurons is not an obstacle to principled credit assignment but the substrate that enables it. The logical progression runs from canonical predictive coding’s point-neuron formulation–which requires dedicated error-coding populations (L2/3) separate from representation-carrying populations (L5/6)–through Urbanczik and Senn’s demonstration that splitting a neuron into just two electrically coupled compartments suffices for local gradient computation, to Sacramento et al.’s three-compartment model in which error is encoded in the apical dendritic voltage of the same neuron whose soma carries the representational signal. Active dendritic conductances then refine this graded mismatch into discrete, high-SNR burst-encoded errors, with the calcium-spike threshold providing a biophysical precision gate. Alongside these instructive signals, each neuron maintains a background error landscape–homeostatic rate errors, self-predictive temporal errors, metabolic cost signals–that constrains the operating regime within which task-driven learning occurs, mirroring at the single-cell level the multi-objective loss described in "Cortical Loss Functions."

These neuronal mechanisms clarify, rather than compete with, the laminar proposals of the preceding subsection. The laminar models specify what populations must exchange what signals across what pathways; the dendritic models specify how individual neurons within those populations physically perform the requisite comparisons. The Sacramento et al. model’s SST-like interneuron cancellation at apical dendrites provides a single-neuron mechanism for the laminar-level operation that Bastos et al. assign to SST+^+ cells and that predictive routing describes as pathway-selective inhibition: in each case, error emerges from the failure of an inhibitory signal to fully cancel descending input. The burst/singlet distinction at the dendritic level maps onto the predicted-vs.-unpredicted dichotomy at the columnar level–the Thousand Brains framework’s sparse-vs.-bursting responses, predictive routing’s differential gamma for unexpected stimuli, Sacramento et al.’s non-zero apical voltage after incomplete cancellation are all manifestations of the same principle at different scales. And if error is encoded in the apical compartment and prediction in the somatic rate of the same neuron, then the laminar-level disagreement over whether L2/3 “is” an error or prediction population is partly resolved: it depends on which readout–dendritic voltage or somatic firing–a given downstream target accesses.

A remaining concern is that the dendritic credit-assignment models operate within chain-like architectures, whereas cortex is a dense, recurrent, skip-connected graph. As discussed in "From Hierarchical Levels to Heterarchical Graphs," Millidge, Tschantz, and Buckley close this gap by proving that predictive coding on an arbitrary computation graph 𝒢={𝕍,𝔼}\mathcal{G} = \{\mathbb{V}, \mathbb{E}\} converges at equilibrium to exact backpropagation gradients–achieved through simultaneous local relaxation rather than sequential backward sweeps, with no weight transport and no designated output layer. The local dendritic comparisons reviewed here therefore do not require strict feedforward organization to perform effective credit assignment. Yet "approximating backprop" remains a lossy abstraction of what cortex actually does: backpropagation presupposes a fixed graph, a single scalar loss, and synchronous phases–none of which hold biologically. The cortex’s computation graph is continuously reconfigured by attention and neuromodulatory state; its loss is distributed, precision-weighted, and temporally deep; and its populations update asynchronously. What the Millidge et al. result establishes is not that cortex implements backprop, but that local prediction-error minimization iterated across an arbitrary graph suffices to recover the gradients backprop computes–and this sufficiency is topology-independent. Backprop is best understood not as the algorithm the brain runs but as a normative upper bound on credit-assignment quality that local, biologically plausible relaxation dynamics can approach on exactly the kind of heterarchical graphs that brains are. The deepest invariant across these proposals is therefore architectural rather than algorithmic: at every synapse in the cortical sheet, the information needed to evaluate local consistency with the global objective is made available by the convergence of feedforward, feedback, and lateral signals onto distinct dendritic compartments–and the mismatch between compartments, read out through calcium- and voltage-dependent mechanisms, provides the error signal that drives learning.
